newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal's Chand, communists make strange bedfellows.
newsitem.headline: Nepal's Chand, communists make strange bedfellows.

text.p: Lokendra Bahadur Chand was the last Nepali prime minister under a partyless democracy system that the kingdom's communists helped to overthrow in 1990.
On Monday, the quiet, rightwing politician staked a claim to form a new government in an uneasy new alliance with communist partners.
The communists joined hands with the Nepali Congress party in 1990 in a popular pro-democracy movement that ousted Chand, widely seen as a pro-royalist leader under an absolute monarch.

Last Friday, it was Chand's decision to withdraw from a 17-month-old Nepali Congress-led coalition that helped to topple the government in a confidence vote, paving the way for his anticipated third term as prime minister.
Suave, softspoken and graying, Chand was first appointed prime minister in 1983, a post he held for more than two years.

The articulate but low-profile politician became prime minister for a second time in 1990 before a bloody pro-democracy movement put an end to the partyless system, which had permitted the king to rule directly over a legislative assembly.
Usually seen wearing a jacket over a kurta-pyjama suit with a Nepali cap, Chand was called "Mr Clean" as prime minister while allegations of corruption were levelled at his ministers.
He and another former prime minister, Surya Bahadur Thapa, formed the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) after multi-party democracy was established seven years ago.
Chand, 57, was chosen to head the parliamentary wing of the party, which includes 19 deputies in the House of Representatives, while Thapa became the party president.

The RPP virtually broke in two last year when the communist opposition offered to back Chand as prime minister if he helped bring down the coalition headed by the Nepali Congress party's Sher Bahadur Deuba.
Chand walked out with his supporters, accusing Deuba of undermining the RPP and its workers, while Thapa remained loyal to the coalition.
Deuba narrowly survived a censure vote last December, but on Friday, at least 10 RPP members defected to the communist side.
Chand says his personal motto is: "Service without expecting the results thereof."

The medium-built, clean-shaven Nepali leader is a graduate in law from the northern Indian city of Dehradun. Chand has written a collection of comedies and a one-act play and enjoys sports and reading.
He is married with four sons and three daughters.
